title: explain a solubility trend in water from the balance of polar and nonpolar parts of a molecule.
stem: A chemist measures how much of each straight-chain alcohol dissolves in 100 mL of water at 20°C. Every alcohol has one polar -OH group at the end of a chain of carbon atoms joined by nonpolar C-H and C-C bonds. Ethanol (2 carbons) mixes with water in any proportion, 1-butanol (4 carbons) dissolves to about 7 g, 1-hexanol (6 carbons) to about 0.6 g, and 1-decanol (10 carbons) to less than 0.01 g. Which statement best explains the trend?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Longer chains contain more -OH groups, which would make hydrogen bonding with water weaker.
choices.rationale: Every alcohol listed has exactly one -OH group, so the number of -OH groups does not change with chain length.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Longer alcohol molecules are heavier, so they sink out of the water solution before they can dissolve.
choices.rationale: Density is not what limits dissolving; the stem gives solubility values, and a heavier molecule can still dissolve if it bonds well with water.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The nonpolar chain cannot form hydrogen bonds with water and disrupts the water's hydrogen-bond network, and this effect grows with chain length until it outweighs the single -OH group.
choices.rationale: Correct: Each alcohol has just one -OH, so the only thing that changes is the length of the nonpolar tail, which interrupts water-water hydrogen bonds without bonding to water.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Water molecules lose their partial charges when they contact long carbon chains, so they stop forming hydrogen bonds with each other.
choices.rationale: Water molecules always keep their partial charges, so the explanation about losing them is not chemistry that occurs.

title: explain a solubility trend in water from the balance of polar and nonpolar parts of a molecule. (variant 1)
stem: Vitamin C has a small carbon ring with four -OH groups and dissolves readily in water. Vitamin A has a long hydrocarbon chain with a single -OH group and dissolves mainly in fats and oils. A person takes large doses of each for several weeks. Excess vitamin C is quickly lost in urine, while vitamin A accumulates in fatty tissue. Which statement best explains the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vitamin C has more carbon atoms, so it is a larger molecule that the kidneys filter out faster.
choices.rationale: Vitamin A has the longer carbon chain, so it is the larger carbon skeleton, and size does not explain water solubility.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vitamin A has stronger covalent bonds than vitamin C, so water cannot break the molecule down.
choices.rationale: The difference comes from polarity, not from bond strength, and covalent bonds inside either vitamin are not broken by water here.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin C forms many hydrogen bonds with water and stays dissolved in body fluids, while vitamin A is mostly nonpolar and associates with the nonpolar interior of fat.
choices.rationale: Correct: Many polar -OH groups give vitamin C hydrogen bonds with water, while vitamin A's long hydrocarbon chain is nonpolar and is excluded from water but compatible with fat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin A carries a net negative charge, which attracts it to the fat cells that carry a positive charge.
choices.rationale: The stem describes vitamin A as nonpolar with a single -OH, not as an ion, and fat cells are not positively charged.

title: explain a solubility trend in water from the balance of polar and nonpolar parts of a molecule. (variant 2)
stem: Two clear solutions are prepared by dissolving 10 g of table salt (NaCl) in one beaker of water and 10 g of sugar (C12H22O11) in another. A conductivity probe shows that the salt solution conducts electricity well and the sugar solution does not conduct. Both solids dissolve completely. Which statement best explains why the sugar solution does not conduct even though the sugar dissolved?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sugar dissolves by forming bonds with water that remove all charge from the water molecules.
choices.rationale: Water molecules keep their partial charges while hydrogen bonding, and conductivity depends on free ions, not on water losing charge.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sugar dissolves because water breaks its covalent bonds into individual atoms, which carry no charge.
choices.rationale: Dissolving sugar does not break covalent bonds within the sugar molecule, so atoms are not released.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sugar is nonpolar, so it dissolves by being trapped between water molecules without any attraction to them.
choices.rationale: Sugar has many polar -OH groups and is not nonpolar, and a nonpolar substance would not dissolve well in water.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sugar stays as intact, uncharged molecules whose many -OH groups form hydrogen bonds with water, so no free ions are produced.
choices.rationale: Correct: Conduction requires free ions; sugar's polar -OH groups hydrogen bond with water so the molecules disperse intact without becoming ions.

title: explain a solubility trend in water from the balance of polar and nonpolar parts of a molecule. (variant 3)
stem: A student shakes olive oil with water in a sealed bottle and sees many tiny oil droplets. After the bottle sits for an hour, the droplets have merged into one layer on top of the water. Which statement best explains why the droplets merge?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oil molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, which pulls the droplets together.
choices.rationale: Oil molecules are nonpolar hydrocarbons and have no -OH groups, so they cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oil molecules are attracted to the partial charges on water molecules and gather at the top.
choices.rationale: Attraction to water's partial charges would keep oil dispersed and mixed in, the opposite of what is observed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gravity pulls the oil droplets together because oil has a higher density than water.
choices.rationale: Oil is less dense than water, which is why the oil layer ends up on top, so density does not explain the merging.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Water molecules hydrogen bond with one another and exclude the nonpolar oil, so merging reduces the oil surface exposed to water.
choices.rationale: Correct: The nonpolar oil cannot hydrogen bond, so water's strong self-attraction pushes oil together into the smallest contact area, which is one layer.

title: connect the density data of liquid water and ice to hydrogen-bond arrangement and to survival of aquatic life.
stem: A pond is monitored through a winter. The density of water is 0.9997 g/mL at 10°C, 1.0000 g/mL at 4°C, 0.9999 g/mL at 1°C, and 0.9998 g/mL for liquid water at 0°C. Ice at 0°C has a density of 0.917 g/mL. In midwinter the pond has a layer of ice at the surface, water near 0°C just under the ice, and water at 4°C at the bottom. Which statement best explains the layering and why the fish can survive?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In ice each molecule is held in an open lattice by stable hydrogen bonds, which makes ice less dense so it floats and insulates the water below, while 4°C water is densest and sinks to the bottom.
choices.rationale: Correct: The data show maximum liquid density at 4°C and a lower density for ice; the hydrogen-bonded open lattice of ice explains why it floats and leaves liquid water beneath.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Water at 4°C has the fewest hydrogen bonds, so it moves downward, and ice forms where bonds are fewest.
choices.rationale: Ice has the most stable hydrogen bonds, not the fewest, and the 4°C water is denser because the molecules are closer together.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ice is less dense because its hydrogen bonds break, spreading the molecules apart, and the surface freezes first because the air is colder.
choices.rationale: Freezing does not break hydrogen bonds; it makes them more stable and fixed, and this explanation reverses the real cause of the lower density.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All water becomes denser as it cools, so the coldest water stays at the bottom and the fish freeze first.
choices.rationale: The density data show that water is densest at 4°C and becomes less dense below that, so the coldest water does not sink to the bottom.

title: connect the density data of liquid water and ice to hydrogen-bond arrangement and to survival of aquatic life. (variant 1)
stem: A rigid sealed glass jar is filled completely with 1000 g of liquid water at 0°C and then placed in a freezer. The density of ice is 0.917 g/mL and that of liquid water at 0°C is about 1.00 g/mL. If the jar were able to expand, by about what amount would the volume change when all the water freezes, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 8% smaller, because the molecules lose energy and pack more tightly.
choices.rationale: This is the pattern for most substances, but water is unusual because ice occupies more volume than the liquid.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 9% larger, because the hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in a fixed open lattice with more space between them.
choices.rationale: Correct: 1000 g divided by 0.917 g/mL is about 1090 mL, which is roughly 9% more than 1000 mL, caused by the open hydrogen-bonded lattice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No change, because the mass of the water stays the same during freezing.
choices.rationale: Mass is conserved, but volume depends on density, which is lower for ice, so the volume does change.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 50% larger, because every molecule forms twice as many covalent bonds in ice.
choices.rationale: Freezing does not form covalent bonds, and the calculation from the densities gives about 9%, not 50%.

title: connect the density data of liquid water and ice to hydrogen-bond arrangement and to survival of aquatic life. (variant 2)
stem: A block of ice at -10°C is heated at a constant rate in an insulated container. The temperature rises steadily to 0°C, then stays at 0°C for several minutes while the heater keeps running, and then rises again once all of the ice has become liquid water. Which statement best explains the flat portion at 0°C?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The added energy breaks the covalent O-H bonds in water molecules, which stops the temperature from rising.
choices.rationale: Melting does not break covalent bonds; water molecules stay as H2O, and only intermolecular hydrogen bonds loosen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The added energy is used to break hydrogen bonds in the ice lattice, so it changes the arrangement of molecules rather than raising their average kinetic energy.
choices.rationale: Correct: A temperature plateau during a phase change shows that energy is being absorbed to disrupt intermolecular hydrogen bonds instead of increasing kinetic energy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The heater stops transferring energy to the sample while the ice is present.
choices.rationale: The heater keeps running, so energy continues to enter the sample, and the flat temperature means that energy is being used for something other than warming.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ice and liquid water have identical energies, so no energy is needed to melt the ice.
choices.rationale: If no energy were needed, the ice would melt instantly and there would be no plateau, but melting does require energy.

title: connect the density data of liquid water and ice to hydrogen-bond arrangement and to survival of aquatic life. (variant 3)
stem: A scientist imagines a planet where the solid form of a hypothetical liquid is denser than its liquid, so the solid sinks. Lakes on the planet cool in winter in the same way as lakes on Earth. Which outcome is most likely for the lakes there?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ice would form only at the surface and protect liquid beneath it, as in Earth lakes.
choices.rationale: Surface ice protecting the water below depends on ice being less dense than liquid, which is not true on this planet.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lakes would never freeze, because the liquid always stays warmer than its surroundings.
choices.rationale: Cooling in winter lowers the temperature to the freezing point, so freezing can occur and the lakes can freeze.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Solid would form at the surface, sink, and accumulate on the bottom, so lakes could freeze from the bottom upward and leave little liquid habitat.
choices.rationale: Correct: A solid denser than its liquid sinks, so it collects at the bottom and the lake can freeze solid, unlike Earth lakes where floating ice insulates the liquid water.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The solid would form at the surface and stay there, because surface water is always colder.
choices.rationale: A solid that is denser than the liquid would not float, so it would not remain at the surface.

title: use radioactive element labels to infer which biological molecules incorporate which elements.
stem: Bacteria are grown for several generations in one of two media, each containing a single radioactive element: Medium 1 has radioactive phosphate, and Medium 2 has radioactive sulfate (which cells convert into sulfur-containing amino acids). Cells are then broken open and their molecules separated by type. In Medium 1 cultures, radioactivity is high in DNA and RNA, moderate in the membrane lipid fraction, and negligible in the polypeptide backbone of proteins and in polysaccharides. In Medium 2 cultures, radioactivity is found in proteins but not in DNA, RNA, lipids, or polysaccharides. Which pair of statements best explains the results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Phosphorus is part of nucleic acids and of the phospholipids in membranes, and sulfur is present in some amino acids but not in nucleic acids or lipids.
choices.rationale: Correct: Phosphorus appears in nucleotides and phospholipids; sulfur appears in cysteine and methionine, so the label pattern identifies P and S.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medium 1 labels molecules that contain carbon, and Medium 2 labels molecules that contain nitrogen.
choices.rationale: Carbon is found in all four classes of molecules, and a carbon label would therefore appear in polysaccharides and every other fraction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phosphorus is part of every amino acid, and sulfur is part of the sugar-phosphate backbone of nucleic acids.
choices.rationale: Amino acids do not contain phosphorus in their basic structure, and the nucleic acid backbone contains phosphate rather than sulfur.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both labels reached cells in equal amounts, so the differences are caused by how quickly each fraction was broken down.
choices.rationale: The stem reports high and negligible values in different fractions, which reflects incorporation into particular molecules rather than any difference in breakdown speed.

title: use radioactive element labels to infer which biological molecules incorporate which elements. (variant 1)
stem: A virus consists of a protein coat surrounding a DNA genome. Two batches of the virus are grown in bacteria: batch 1 in medium with radioactive sulfur, and batch 2 in medium with radioactive phosphorus. Purified virus from each batch is then used to infect new bacteria. After infection, the bacteria are separated from the empty coats, and radioactivity is measured in the bacterial pellet. Which result is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both batches give a strongly radioactive pellet, because sulfur and phosphorus are both in DNA.
choices.rationale: DNA does not contain sulfur, so a sulfur label could not be found in the DNA that entered the bacteria.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Batch 1 gives a strongly radioactive pellet, because DNA contains sulfur and enters the bacteria.
choices.rationale: Sulfur is in some amino acids of the coat protein, not in DNA, so the sulfur label stays with the coats.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Batch 2 gives a strongly radioactive pellet, because DNA contains phosphorus and enters the bacteria, while the sulfur-labeled coats stay outside.
choices.rationale: Correct: DNA carries phosphorus but no sulfur, and in this experiment the DNA enters the cells while the protein coats remain outside, so the phosphorus label is found in the pellet.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither batch gives a radioactive pellet, because the labeled elements are lost when the virus replicates.
choices.rationale: The labeled DNA entering the cells is a physical part of the infection, so its phosphorus label remains measurable in the pellet.

title: use radioactive element labels to infer which biological molecules incorporate which elements. (variant 2)
stem: Algae are grown for several generations in a medium whose only nitrogen source is a heavy isotope of nitrogen (15N). The cells are then broken open and the following molecules are purified and compared with those from algae grown in normal nitrogen: triglycerides, cellulose, proteins, and DNA. Which purified molecules are expected to be heavier than normal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Triglycerides and DNA, because both store energy and information in long chains.
choices.rationale: Triglycerides contain only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, so they would not take up the heavy nitrogen label even though they store energy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cellulose and proteins, because both are structural polymers.
choices.rationale: Cellulose is a polymer of glucose containing no nitrogen, so structural function does not determine nitrogen content.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All four molecules, because every biological molecule contains nitrogen.
choices.rationale: Carbohydrates and triglycerides contain no nitrogen, so not every molecule would be heavier.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Proteins and DNA, because amino acids and nucleotide bases contain nitrogen, whereas triglycerides and cellulose do not.
choices.rationale: Correct: Nitrogen is in the amino group of amino acids and in the bases of nucleotides, but triglycerides and cellulose contain only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.

title: use radioactive element labels to infer which biological molecules incorporate which elements. (variant 3)
stem: Yeast cells are given radioactive phosphate for one hour. The cells are then separated into four purified molecule groups: ATP, DNA, phospholipids, and the glucose in the medium that was taken up by the cells. Which groups should contain the label?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ATP, DNA, and phospholipids, because each contains phosphate groups.
choices.rationale: Correct: ATP, DNA backbones, and phospholipid heads each contain phosphate, while glucose is made of only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA only, because phosphate is used only for genetic information.
choices.rationale: Phosphate is also in ATP and in the heads of phospholipids, so the label would not be limited to DNA.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose and phospholipids, because they supply energy and phosphate to the cell.
choices.rationale: Glucose has no phosphorus, so it could not carry a phosphate label, even though cells use it as a fuel.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All four groups, because glucose is converted into phosphate by the cell.
choices.rationale: Cells do not convert glucose into phosphate, because phosphorus is an element that cannot be made from carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.

title: assign macromolecule classes from elemental composition data.
stem: A laboratory analyzes four purified biological samples and reports the percent by mass of each element. Sample W: carbon 40.0, hydrogen 6.7, oxygen 53.3. Sample X: carbon 77, hydrogen 12, oxygen 11. Sample Y: carbon 52, hydrogen 7, oxygen 23, nitrogen 16, sulfur 2. Sample Z: carbon 35, hydrogen 4, oxygen 33, nitrogen 19, phosphorus 9. Which assignment of samples to macromolecule class is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: W is a carbohydrate, X is a lipid, Y is a protein, and Z is a nucleic acid.
choices.rationale: Correct: W has the 1:2:1 ratio of C:H:O in carbohydrates, X is very low in oxygen like a fat, sulfur in Y fits protein, and nitrogen plus phosphorus in Z fits a nucleic acid.

choices.label: B
choices.text: W is a protein, X is a nucleic acid, Y is a carbohydrate, and Z is a lipid.
choices.rationale: Carbohydrates and lipids contain no nitrogen, so Y with 16 percent nitrogen cannot be a carbohydrate and Z cannot be a lipid.

choices.label: C
choices.text: W is a lipid, X is a carbohydrate, Y is a protein, and Z is a nucleic acid.
choices.rationale: The sample with almost no oxygen is the lipid and the sample with a 1:2:1 ratio of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen is the carbohydrate, which reverses W and X.

choices.label: D
choices.text: W is a carbohydrate, X is a lipid, Y is a nucleic acid, and Z is a protein.
choices.rationale: Phosphorus is part of the sugar-phosphate backbone of nucleic acids and is not part of the amino acids in proteins, so Y and Z are reversed.

title: assign macromolecule classes from elemental composition data. (variant 1)
stem: Four samples are analyzed. Sample Q: carbon 63, hydrogen 10, oxygen 21, nitrogen 2, phosphorus 4. Sample R: carbon 36, hydrogen 4, oxygen 33, nitrogen 19, phosphorus 8. Sample S: carbon 53, hydrogen 7, oxygen 24, nitrogen 15, sulfur 1. Sample T: carbon 44.4, hydrogen 6.2, oxygen 49.4. Which assignment is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Q is a nucleic acid, R is a phospholipid, S is a protein, and T is a polysaccharide.
choices.rationale: Nucleic acids have a high nitrogen percentage from their bases, whereas the low nitrogen and high carbon in Q fits a phospholipid, so the pair is reversed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Q is a phospholipid, R is a nucleic acid, S is a protein, and T is a polysaccharide.
choices.rationale: Correct: Q has high carbon with a little nitrogen and phosphorus (a phospholipid head with long carbon chains), R has high nitrogen with phosphorus (nucleic acid), S has nitrogen and sulfur (protein), and T is C:H:O near 1:2:1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Q is a protein, R is a nucleic acid, S is a phospholipid, and T is a polysaccharide.
choices.rationale: Sample S contains sulfur but no phosphorus and is a better match for protein, while Q with high carbon and phosphorus is not a protein.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Q is a phospholipid, R is a protein, S is a nucleic acid, and T is a lipid.
choices.rationale: T has hydrogen and oxygen in about a 2:1 ratio like a carbohydrate, and lipids have much less oxygen.

title: assign macromolecule classes from elemental composition data. (variant 2)
stem: A purified polypeptide from a bacterium is analyzed and found to contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen, but no sulfur. A student concludes that the sample cannot be a protein because "all proteins contain sulfur." Which response is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The student is correct, because sulfur forms the peptide bonds that join amino acids.
choices.rationale: Peptide bonds form between a carboxyl carbon and an amino nitrogen and contain no sulfur.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The student is correct, because the nitrogen in the sample shows that it is a nucleic acid instead.
choices.rationale: Nucleic acids contain phosphorus, and the lack of phosphorus here suggests it is not a nucleic acid; nitrogen alone does not separate the classes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The student is incorrect, because sulfur is in the amino group of every amino acid.
choices.rationale: The amino group contains nitrogen and hydrogen, and sulfur appears only in the R groups of a few amino acids.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The student is incorrect, because sulfur is found only in the R groups of the amino acids cysteine and methionine, so a protein lacking those amino acids has no sulfur.
choices.rationale: Correct: Only two of the 20 amino acids, cysteine and methionine, contain sulfur, so a polypeptide without them can lack sulfur and remain a protein.

title: assign macromolecule classes from elemental composition data. (variant 3)
stem: A lipid extract from a cell membrane is analyzed and found to contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and a small amount of nitrogen. A fat extract from a seed contains only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Which statement best explains the difference between the two extracts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The membrane lipid is a triglyceride, and the seed fat is a phospholipid.
choices.rationale: This is reversed, because triglycerides lack phosphorus and the seed fat with only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen matches a triglyceride.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The nitrogen and phosphorus in the membrane lipid come from its long hydrocarbon chains.
choices.rationale: Hydrocarbon chains are made of carbon and hydrogen only, so they cannot be the source of nitrogen or phosphorus.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The membrane lipid is a phospholipid with a phosphate-containing head group, often with a nitrogen-containing group, whereas a triglyceride has only glycerol and fatty acids.
choices.rationale: Correct: Phospholipid heads add phosphate and often a nitrogenous group such as choline, whereas triglycerides consist only of glycerol and fatty acids, which contain only C, H, and O.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The membrane lipid contains amino acids, which a seed fat lacks.
choices.rationale: A membrane lipid does not contain amino acids or peptide bonds, and its nitrogen comes from a small head group.

title: account for the mass of water lost in dehydration synthesis when calculating the mass of a polymer.
stem: A linear polysaccharide is built by dehydration synthesis from 12 glucose monomers. Each free glucose molecule has a molar mass of 180 g/mol, and each water molecule released has a molar mass of 18 g/mol. What is the molar mass of the polymer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1962 g/mol, because 11 bonds form and 11 water molecules are released.
choices.rationale: Correct: 12 x 180 = 2160 g/mol for the monomers; a linear chain of 12 has 11 bonds, so subtract 11 x 18 = 198, giving 1962 g/mol.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2160 g/mol, because the polymer has the same mass as its 12 monomers added together.
choices.rationale: This ignores that each dehydration reaction releases a water molecule, so the polymer is lighter than its monomers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1944 g/mol, because one water molecule is released for each of the 12 monomers.
choices.rationale: A linear chain of 12 monomers has 11 bonds, not 12, so only 11 waters are lost.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 2358 g/mol, because each bond that forms adds one water molecule to the polymer.
choices.rationale: Dehydration synthesis removes water from the monomers rather than adding it, so this reverses the direction of the mass change.

title: account for the mass of water lost in dehydration synthesis when calculating the mass of a polymer. (variant 1)
stem: A cell links 10 amino acids, with an average molar mass of 120 g/mol each, into a linear polypeptide. Each peptide bond formed releases one water molecule (18 g/mol). What is the molar mass of the polypeptide?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1200 g/mol
choices.rationale: This is the sum of the free amino acids and ignores the water that leaves with each peptide bond.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1020 g/mol
choices.rationale: This subtracts 10 waters (180), but a linear chain of 10 amino acids has only 9 peptide bonds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1038 g/mol
choices.rationale: Correct: 10 x 120 = 1200 g/mol; 9 peptide bonds release 9 x 18 = 162 g/mol of water, so the polypeptide is 1200 - 162 = 1038 g/mol.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1362 g/mol
choices.rationale: This adds 162 to the monomer total, which treats dehydration synthesis as adding water rather than removing it.

title: account for the mass of water lost in dehydration synthesis when calculating the mass of a polymer. (variant 2)
stem: A linear polymer has a measured molar mass of 2658 g/mol. It was made by dehydration synthesis from identical monomers, each with a molar mass of 150 g/mol, and one water molecule (18 g/mol) was released for each bond. How many monomers does the polymer contain?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Dividing 2658 by 150 gives about 17.7, which ignores the water lost in forming the bonds.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: 22 monomers would give 22 x 150 - 21 x 18 = 2922 g/mol, which is larger than the measured mass.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: 19 is the number of bonds in the chain of 20 monomers, not the number of monomers.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: For n monomers the mass is 150n - 18(n - 1) = 132n + 18; setting this equal to 2658 gives n = 20.

title: account for the mass of water lost in dehydration synthesis when calculating the mass of a polymer. (variant 3)
stem: A linear polymer with a molar mass of 3000 g/mol contains 24 monomers. Complete hydrolysis converts it into 24 free monomers by adding water at every bond (18 g/mol per water). What is the total molar mass of the 24 free monomers?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 3000 g/mol, because mass is conserved and the monomers have the same mass as the polymer.
choices.rationale: Hydrolysis adds water, so the products include the mass of the added water and the monomers together weigh more than the polymer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3414 g/mol, because 23 water molecules are added.
choices.rationale: Correct: A chain of 24 monomers has 23 bonds, so hydrolysis adds 23 x 18 = 414 g/mol of water: 3000 + 414 = 3414 g/mol.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 2586 g/mol, because the monomers are smaller than the polymer.
choices.rationale: This subtracts the water mass, but hydrolysis adds water rather than removing it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 3432 g/mol, because 24 water molecules are added.
choices.rationale: This uses 24 bonds, but a linear chain of 24 monomers has only 23 bonds.

title: distinguish true polymers from large molecules built by dehydration synthesis that are not polymers.
stem: Four purified samples are completely hydrolyzed and the products are identified. Sample 1 gives only one kind of six-carbon sugar, with many molecules per original molecule. Sample 2 gives many molecules from about 20 kinds of compounds that each have an amino group and a carboxyl group. Sample 3 gives four kinds of compounds, each with a nitrogenous base, a sugar, and phosphate. Sample 4 gives, per original molecule, one three-carbon alcohol and three long-chain fatty acids. Which sample is NOT a polymer made of a long chain of repeating monomers, even though it was assembled by dehydration synthesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sample 1, because it contains only one type of monomer.
choices.rationale: A polysaccharide made from one type of monomer is still a polymer, since many identical units are linked by dehydration synthesis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sample 4, because it is assembled from glycerol and three fatty acids rather than a chain of repeating monomers.
choices.rationale: Correct: Samples 1 to 3 break down into many repeating monomers (monosaccharides, amino acids, nucleotides), but a triglyceride is built from one glycerol and three fatty acids.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sample 2, because it contains more than one kind of monomer.
choices.rationale: Proteins are polymers even though they contain about 20 types of amino acid monomers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sample 3, because its products contain three different parts.
choices.rationale: Each nucleotide has three parts, but nucleic acids are chains of many nucleotide monomers and are polymers.

title: distinguish true polymers from large molecules built by dehydration synthesis that are not polymers. (variant 1)
stem: A student says: "A triglyceride is a polymer, because three fatty acids are joined to glycerol by three dehydration reactions and hydrolysis gives smaller units back." Which response is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The student is partly correct about the reactions, but a triglyceride is not a polymer, because it is not a long chain of repeated similar monomers.
choices.rationale: Correct: Triglycerides do form by dehydration synthesis and break by hydrolysis, but they consist of one glycerol and three fatty acids, which is not a chain of repeating monomers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The student is correct, because any molecule formed by dehydration synthesis is a polymer.
choices.rationale: Dehydration synthesis alone does not make a polymer, since a polymer needs many repeated monomers linked in a chain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The student is incorrect, because triglycerides form without any dehydration synthesis.
choices.rationale: Ester bonds in triglycerides are formed by dehydration synthesis, with release of water.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The student is incorrect, because a triglyceride is too small to be a molecule at all.
choices.rationale: A triglyceride is a molecule, and the problem with calling it a polymer is its structure, not whether it is a molecule.

title: distinguish true polymers from large molecules built by dehydration synthesis that are not polymers. (variant 2)
stem: Complete hydrolysis of an unknown large molecule yields about 20 different small compounds. Every one of them contains an amino group and a carboxyl group, differs only in the group attached to the central carbon, and the products contain no phosphorus. Which statement is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The molecule is a nucleic acid, because the products contain nitrogen.
choices.rationale: Nucleotides contain phosphate and a nitrogenous base, and no phosphorus was found in these products.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The molecule is a protein, a polymer of amino acid monomers joined by peptide bonds.
choices.rationale: Correct: Monomers with an amino group, a carboxyl group, and a variable side chain are amino acids, and polymers of amino acids are proteins.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The molecule is a polysaccharide, because it is large and breaks into small units.
choices.rationale: Monosaccharide monomers contain carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen only, so they lack amino groups.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The molecule is a phospholipid, because the products have both polar and nonpolar groups.
choices.rationale: Phospholipids hydrolyze into glycerol, fatty acids, and a phosphate group, and these products are not amino acids.

title: distinguish true polymers from large molecules built by dehydration synthesis that are not polymers. (variant 3)
stem: A cell extract contains a polysaccharide, a polypeptide, a DNA strand, and a triglyceride. Complete hydrolysis of each releases its building blocks. Which pairing of molecule and the products of its hydrolysis is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The polysaccharide releases nucleotides.
choices.rationale: Polysaccharides are polymers of monosaccharides, and nucleotides come from nucleic acids.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The polypeptide releases glycerol and fatty acids.
choices.rationale: Polypeptides break down to amino acids, and glycerol and fatty acids come from triglycerides.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The DNA strand releases nucleotides.
choices.rationale: Correct: A nucleic acid is a polymer of nucleotides, so hydrolysis of a DNA strand releases nucleotides.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The triglyceride releases amino acids.
choices.rationale: Triglycerides break down to glycerol and fatty acids, and amino acids come from the hydrolysis of proteins.

title: explain enzyme specificity toward glucose polymers by the orientation of the glycosidic linkage.
stem: An enzyme preparation called amylase is added to four glucose-containing substances and incubated. Results: starch (glucose units linked alpha-1,4) is broken into maltose and glucose; glycogen (alpha-1,4 and alpha-1,6 links) is broken into maltose and glucose; maltose (two glucose units linked alpha-1,4) is broken into glucose; and cellulose (glucose units linked beta-1,4) shows no breakdown. Which hypothesis best explains the results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cellulose contains a monomer other than glucose, so the enzyme cannot recognize it.
choices.rationale: The stem states cellulose consists of glucose units, so a different monomer does not explain the result.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The amylase active site fits alpha-linked glucose, and the beta-1,4 linkage in cellulose has a different orientation that does not fit the active site.
choices.rationale: Correct: All four substances contain glucose, and the enzyme acts on all with alpha linkages but not on beta linkages, so the specificity depends on linkage orientation and active site shape.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cellulose has no covalent bonds between glucose units, so there is nothing for the enzyme to break.
choices.rationale: Cellulose is held together by covalent beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds, and hydrogen bonds between chains are not the bonds linking monomers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cellulose molecules are too small for the enzyme to bind.
choices.rationale: Cellulose is a very long polymer, so size is not what prevents the enzyme from acting.

title: explain enzyme specificity toward glucose polymers by the orientation of the glycosidic linkage. (variant 1)
stem: A cow is fed only grass, whose carbohydrate is mostly cellulose, and it gains weight normally. A second cow receives the same diet along with an antibiotic that kills most of the microorganisms in its rumen, and it loses weight. Mammals do not produce enzymes that cleave beta-1,4 glucose linkages. Which statement best explains the results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotics destroy the cow's own amylase, which digests cellulose.
choices.rationale: Amylase cuts alpha-1,4 links in starch and does not digest cellulose, and antibiotics act on microorganisms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cellulose in grass is made of amino acids that the antibiotic prevents the cow from absorbing.
choices.rationale: Cellulose is a polymer of glucose, not amino acids, so this describes the wrong molecule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The antibiotic changes cellulose into starch, which the cow cannot digest.
choices.rationale: Antibiotics do not chemically convert cellulose to starch, and the weight loss results from the loss of microbial enzymes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rumen microorganisms provide enzymes that hydrolyze the beta-1,4 linkages of cellulose, releasing glucose the cow can use.
choices.rationale: Correct: The cow lacks enzymes for beta-1,4 linkages; microbes supply them, and when the microbes are killed the cow cannot release glucose from cellulose.

title: explain enzyme specificity toward glucose polymers by the orientation of the glycosidic linkage. (variant 2)
stem: A person drinks milk and develops digestive distress. The person digests starch and table sugar (sucrose) normally. Milk sugar is lactose, a disaccharide of glucose and galactose joined by a beta-1,4 linkage. Tests show the person's intestinal cells do not make lactase, the enzyme that cleaves this linkage. Which statement best explains why the person digests starch but not lactose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each digestive enzyme fits a particular sugar and linkage, so enzymes for alpha-linked starch and for sucrose cannot substitute for lactase.
choices.rationale: Correct: Enzyme specificity depends on the shape of the active site, so a specific enzyme is required for each linkage and sugar, and lactase is missing here.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lactose is a polysaccharide that is too long for any enzyme to cut.
choices.rationale: Lactose is a disaccharide, and its small size is not what prevents digestion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The enzymes that digest starch and sucrose can cut any glycosidic bond, so lactose should be digested the same way.
choices.rationale: Enzymes are specific for their substrates, so enzymes for starch and sucrose do not cut the beta-1,4 bond in lactose.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactose contains no glucose, so it cannot be hydrolyzed.
choices.rationale: Lactose contains a glucose unit, and the problem is a missing enzyme rather than missing glucose.

title: explain enzyme specificity toward glucose polymers by the orientation of the glycosidic linkage. (variant 3)
stem: Two unknown polymers, P and Q, are each made only of glucose. Polymer P is hydrolyzed by cellulase but not by amylase. Polymer Q is hydrolyzed by amylase but not by cellulase. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: P has alpha-1,4 linkages and Q has beta-1,4 linkages.
choices.rationale: This reverses the assignments, since cellulase cuts beta-1,4 links and amylase cuts alpha-1,4 links.

choices.label: B
choices.text: P and Q have identical structures, because both are made only of glucose.
choices.rationale: Identical monomers do not mean identical structure, as the different enzyme results show different linkages.

choices.label: C
choices.text: P and Q differ because P contains a different monomer than Q.
choices.rationale: The stem states both are made only of glucose, so the monomers are the same.

choices.label: D
choices.text: P has beta-1,4 linkages like cellulose and Q has alpha-1,4 linkages like starch, so they differ in linkage orientation.
choices.rationale: Correct: Each enzyme cuts one linkage orientation, so the opposite results show that the two polymers have different glycosidic linkages despite identical monomers.

title: relate branching of a glucose polymer to the number of chain ends and the rate of glucose release.
stem: Two storage polymers each contain 10,000 glucose units. Polymer L is unbranched and has one end where glucose is removed. Polymer H has a branch about every 10 glucose units, which gives it about 1,001 chain ends. An enzyme removes glucose only from the ends of chains, one unit at a time, and each end is processed at the same rate. How does the initial rate of glucose release from H compare with that from L?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About the same, because both polymers contain 10,000 glucose units.
choices.rationale: The total number of glucose units is the same, but the enzyme acts on ends, so the rate depends on how many ends are available.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 1,000 times faster, because H has about 1,001 ends for the enzyme to act on, compared with 1 end in L.
choices.rationale: Correct: Rate scales with the number of ends: 1,001 ends versus 1 end gives about 1,000 times the initial rate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 10 times faster, because H has a branch every 10 units.
choices.rationale: The branch spacing of 10 units is not the ratio of ends, and 10,000 units with a branch every 10 give about 1,000 ends.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 10 times slower, because branching makes H more compact.
choices.rationale: Branching increases the number of ends, so a compact shape does not slow release at each end.

title: relate branching of a glucose polymer to the number of chain ends and the rate of glucose release. (variant 1)
stem: Muscle glycogen has a branch about every 10 glucose units, while plant amylopectin has a branch about every 25 units. A 5,000-unit molecule of each has one more chain end than its number of branches (glycogen about 501 ends, amylopectin about 201 ends). Assuming an enzyme removes glucose only from chain ends at equal rates per end, how does the initial release rate from glycogen compare with that from amylopectin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 0.4 times as fast, because the glycogen is more compact.
choices.rationale: This is the reciprocal of the ratio and treats more ends as slowing release.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 25 times faster, because glycogen has 25 minus 10 more branches.
choices.rationale: Subtracting the branch spacings does not give the ratio of ends, which is 501 to 201.

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 2.5 times faster for glycogen, in proportion to the number of ends.
choices.rationale: Correct: 501 ends divided by 201 ends is about 2.5, so glycogen is mobilized about 2.5 times faster.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The same, because both molecules contain 5,000 glucose units.
choices.rationale: Equal glucose content does not make the rates equal, because the enzyme acts at ends and the polymers have different numbers of ends.

title: relate branching of a glucose polymer to the number of chain ends and the rate of glucose release. (variant 2)
stem: A mutant mouse cannot make the enzyme that creates branch points in glycogen, so its glycogen is long and mostly unbranched. During a short burst of intense running, the mouse's glycogen supply is the same size as in a normal mouse. Which outcome is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Faster release of glucose, because longer chains are easier for enzymes to process.
choices.rationale: Fewer ends means fewer sites for the enzyme, so longer chains do not speed release.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Slower release of glucose during the burst, because there are fewer chain ends where enzymes can remove glucose.
choices.rationale: Correct: Rapid glucose release depends on many ends, and unbranched glycogen has far fewer ends, so mobilization is slower for a short burst.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No difference, because the amount of stored glucose determines the release rate.
choices.rationale: The stem says the amount of stored glucose is equal, but release rate depends on how many ends are available, not on total amount.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release of fructose, because unbranched chains are converted to a different sugar.
choices.rationale: Removing branches does not convert glucose into another sugar; the monomer stays glucose.

title: relate branching of a glucose polymer to the number of chain ends and the rate of glucose release. (variant 3)
stem: A polysaccharide of 8,000 glucose units has a branch about every 12 units (about 667 chain ends). A mutation shortens the spacing to a branch about every 6 units (about 1,333 chain ends). If an enzyme removes glucose from ends at a constant rate per end, how does the initial release rate change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It roughly doubles, in proportion to the number of ends.
choices.rationale: Correct: Ends increase from about 667 to about 1,333, which is a factor of two, so the release rate roughly doubles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is halved, because shorter branches hold less glucose.
choices.rationale: More branches means more ends, so the release rate rises rather than falls.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is unchanged, because the same 8,000 units are present.
choices.rationale: Total glucose is unchanged but rate depends on the number of ends.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It rises about sixfold, because the spacing changed from 12 to 6 units.
choices.rationale: Halving the spacing doubles the number of ends, so the rate changes by a factor of about two, not six.

title: predict how a lipid's polar and nonpolar regions determine its arrangement in water.
stem: Equal amounts of three lipids are added to separate tubes of water and shaken. Phospholipid: forms a cloudy mixture of tiny sacs, each enclosing a droplet of water. Triglyceride: forms oily droplets that merge into a layer on top and shows no ordered structure. Which statement best explains why the triglyceride does not assemble like the phospholipid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The triglyceride has a larger mass than the phospholipid, so it sinks.
choices.rationale: The triglyceride floats on top, which shows it is less dense than water, so mass is not the cause.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The triglyceride has fewer fatty acid tails than the phospholipid, so it cannot form droplets.
choices.rationale: A triglyceride has three fatty acid tails and a phospholipid has two, so the triglyceride does not have fewer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The triglyceride is hydrophilic, so it dissolves completely in water.
choices.rationale: If the triglyceride were hydrophilic it would dissolve, but the observed layer of merged droplets shows it is hydrophobic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The triglyceride has no polar head group, so the whole molecule is nonpolar and is excluded from water, whereas the phospholipid has a polar phosphate-containing head and nonpolar tails.
choices.rationale: Correct: A triglyceride is entirely nonpolar, so it separates from water as a layer, but a phospholipid is amphipathic and its polar head faces water while tails face each other.

title: predict how a lipid's polar and nonpolar regions determine its arrangement in water. (variant 1)
stem: Phospholipids are mixed with water to form small vesicles, each with a bilayer wall surrounding a water-filled interior. A water-soluble blue dye and a nonpolar red dye are added to the mixture, and the vesicles are then separated and examined. Which result is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The blue dye is in the bilayer interior and the red dye is in the water-filled interior.
choices.rationale: This reverses the placement, as a polar dye would not be found among nonpolar tails.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The blue dye is in the water-filled interior and the surrounding water, and the red dye is in the nonpolar fatty acid region of the bilayer.
choices.rationale: Correct: Polar molecules stay in water, while a nonpolar dye dissolves among the hydrophobic fatty acid tails in the middle of the bilayer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both dyes are in the water-filled interior, because they are small molecules.
choices.rationale: A nonpolar dye is not soluble in water, so it would not remain in the aqueous interior.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither dye associates with the vesicle, because dyes cannot cross a bilayer.
choices.rationale: A nonpolar dye can dissolve in the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer, so it does associate with the vesicles.

title: predict how a lipid's polar and nonpolar regions determine its arrangement in water. (variant 2)
stem: A tube holds a layer of olive oil above a layer of water, and a small amount of phospholipid is added and the tube is shaken. Tiny oil droplets form and remain suspended in the water. Which arrangement of the phospholipid molecules at the surface of an oil droplet best explains the stable droplets?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fatty acid tails face the oil inside the droplet and phosphate heads face the surrounding water.
choices.rationale: Correct: The tails are nonpolar and stay in oil, while the polar heads contact water, which makes the droplets stable and keeps them from merging.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Phosphate heads face the oil and fatty acid tails face the water.
choices.rationale: Polar heads would not favor contact with nonpolar oil, and tails would not favor contact with water.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phospholipids lie flat on the droplet with heads and tails both facing the water.
choices.rationale: Tails are nonpolar, so they would not be exposed to water by lying flat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phospholipids are dissolved in the oil as individual molecules and do not reach the surface.
choices.rationale: Phospholipids are amphipathic and accumulate at the oil-water interface rather than dissolving entirely in the oil.

title: predict how a lipid's polar and nonpolar regions determine its arrangement in water. (variant 3)
stem: Phospholipids are dissolved in a nonpolar liquid, hexane, and a few drops of water are added. Small spherical structures form, each trapping a tiny water droplet. Which arrangement best explains the structures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Phosphate heads face the hexane and tails surround the water droplet.
choices.rationale: Heads are polar and would avoid hexane, and tails would not surround water.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Phosphate heads face the water droplet in the center and fatty acid tails extend into the hexane.
choices.rationale: Correct: In a nonpolar solvent the polar heads cluster around the water and the tails extend into the hexane, the reverse of the arrangement in water.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phospholipids form a double layer with water on both sides of it.
choices.rationale: A bilayer with water on both sides forms in water, but here the surrounding liquid is hexane.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phospholipids join the water droplet by covalent bonds between the tails and the water molecules.
choices.rationale: The interactions are hydrogen bonds between heads and water and hydrophobic effects, not covalent bonds between tails and water.

title: quantify why organisms store energy as fat rather than carbohydrate.
stem: A bear must obtain 36,000 kcal from stored energy during hibernation. Fat provides about 9 kcal per gram and carbohydrate provides about 4 kcal per gram. If the bear stored the same energy as carbohydrate rather than fat, how much more stored mass would it need, and what feature of the molecules explains the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 4 times as much mass, because carbohydrate is a polymer and fat is not.
choices.rationale: 4 is the energy per gram of carbohydrate, not the ratio of masses, which is 9 to 4.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 0.44 times as much mass, because carbohydrate has more oxygen to release energy.
choices.rationale: This is the inverse of the ratio and mistakes extra oxygen for extra energy, since oxygen content lowers energy per gram.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The same mass, because both are made of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
choices.rationale: Both contain C, H, and O, but the proportions differ, and fats contain far more C-H bonds per gram.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 2.25 times as much mass, because fat has more carbon-hydrogen bonds per gram and is less oxidized.
choices.rationale: Correct: Fat needs 36,000 / 9 = 4,000 g and carbohydrate needs 36,000 / 4 = 9,000 g, a ratio of 2.25; fats are rich in C-H bonds that store more energy per gram.

title: quantify why organisms store energy as fat rather than carbohydrate. (variant 1)
stem: A migrating bird stores 200 g of fat for its flight. Fat provides about 9 kcal per gram, and carbohydrate provides about 4 kcal per gram. What mass of carbohydrate would hold the same energy?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Carbohydrate has less energy per gram, so an equal mass would hold less energy.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This multiplies by 4, and the correct approach converts to kcal and then divides by 4 kcal/g.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: 200 g x 9 kcal/g = 1,800 kcal; 1,800 / 4 = 450 g of carbohydrate.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This uses 200 x 4 / 9, which is the inverse of the ratio and gives too small a mass.

title: quantify why organisms store energy as fat rather than carbohydrate. (variant 2)
stem: Sunflower plants store energy in seeds as oil, while many large-seeded grasses store energy as starch. A biologist notes that seeds dispersed by wind or by small animals are often rich in oil. Which statement best explains the advantage of storing oil in small seeds?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oil is more soluble in water and therefore reaches the embryo more rapidly.
choices.rationale: Oil is nonpolar and not soluble in water, so this explanation reverses the property.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oil is lighter than water and therefore floats the seed to new places.
choices.rationale: Floating in water is not the advantage being described for dispersal on land by wind or animals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oil has a high number of C-H bonds per gram, so a small light seed can hold more energy for the embryo.
choices.rationale: Correct: Fats pack about twice the energy per gram of starch, so a seed can carry enough energy for germination while remaining small and light.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oil contains nitrogen, which provides additional energy for germination.
choices.rationale: Triglycerides contain only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen and have no nitrogen.

title: quantify why organisms store energy as fat rather than carbohydrate. (variant 3)
stem: Glycogen is stored with about 2 g of water per gram of glycogen, while fat is stored with almost no water. Using 4 kcal per gram for dry glycogen and 9 kcal per gram for fat, about how many times more energy per gram of stored tissue does fat provide than hydrated glycogen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 2.25 times, as with dry glycogen.
choices.rationale: This is the dry-mass comparison and ignores the water mass stored with the glycogen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 3 times, because the water adds mass.
choices.rationale: 9 divided by 3 is not the comparison, because the energy in the hydrated tissue is 4 kcal in 3 g, not 4 kcal per 1 g.

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 0.15 times, because water stores energy.
choices.rationale: Water does not store usable energy and only adds mass, so this makes the ratio smaller than one.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 6.75 times, because hydrated glycogen provides only about 1.33 kcal per gram.
choices.rationale: Correct: One gram of glycogen with 2 g of water is 3 g containing 4 kcal, or 1.33 kcal per gram; 9 / 1.33 is about 6.75.

title: predict thermal stability of double-stranded DNA from the number of hydrogen bonds.
stem: Three double-stranded DNA fragments, each 20 base pairs long, are heated slowly until the strands separate (melting temperature). Fragment P has 4 G-C pairs and has a melting temperature of 48°C. Fragment Q has 10 G-C pairs and melts at 60°C. Fragment R has 16 G-C pairs and melts at 70°C. A G-C pair has three hydrogen bonds and an A-T pair has two. A new 20-base-pair fragment has 13 G-C pairs. Which melting temperature is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Below 48°C, because the new fragment has more G-C pairs than P.
choices.rationale: More G-C pairs means more hydrogen bonds and greater stability, so the melting temperature should rise, not fall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 60°C, because all 20-base-pair fragments melt at the same temperature.
choices.rationale: The fragments are the same length but melt at different temperatures, which shows that base composition matters.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Between 60°C and 70°C, because it has 53 hydrogen bonds, between Q (50) and R (56).
choices.rationale: Correct: Hydrogen bonds are 13 x 3 + 7 x 2 = 53, between Q at 50 and R at 56, so the melting temperature should lie between 60°C and 70°C.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Above 70°C, because any fragment with more than 10 G-C pairs melts above R.
choices.rationale: The new fragment has fewer G-C pairs than R and so fewer hydrogen bonds, so it should melt below R.

title: predict thermal stability of double-stranded DNA from the number of hydrogen bonds. (variant 1)
stem: Two 20-nucleotide primers are designed to bind a target DNA strand. Primer 1 has 8 G-C pairs when bound, and primer 2 has 14 G-C pairs when bound. The remaining pairs are A-T. Which statement best predicts which duplex requires a higher temperature to separate and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Primer 1's duplex, because A-T pairs have more hydrogen bonds than G-C pairs.
choices.rationale: G-C pairs have three hydrogen bonds and A-T pairs have two, so this reverses the numbers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both duplexes separate at the same temperature, because both are 20 base pairs long.
choices.rationale: Equal length does not mean equal stability when the base composition differs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Primer 1's duplex, because it has more A-T pairs and A-T pairs are covalent bonds.
choices.rationale: Base pairs are held together by hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds, and A-T pairs are weaker.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primer 2's duplex, because it has 14 G-C pairs, giving 54 hydrogen bonds compared with 48 for primer 1.
choices.rationale: Correct: Primer 1 has 8 x 3 + 12 x 2 = 48 hydrogen bonds and primer 2 has 14 x 3 + 6 x 2 = 54, so primer 2 duplex needs more energy to separate.

title: predict thermal stability of double-stranded DNA from the number of hydrogen bonds. (variant 2)
stem: Genomic DNA from two bacterial species is double-stranded. In species X, 31% of bases are adenine. In species Y, 17% of bases are adenine. Both genomes are heated slowly. Which statement is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Species X has the higher melting temperature, because it has more adenine.
choices.rationale: Adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds, so more adenine means a lower melting temperature.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both melt at the same temperature, because both genomes are double-stranded DNA.
choices.rationale: Both are double-stranded DNA, but they differ in base composition and therefore in the hydrogen bonds per base pair.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Species X has the higher melting temperature, because it has 38% G plus C.
choices.rationale: Species X has 38% G plus C, which is less than species Y at 66%, so its melting temperature is lower.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Species Y has the higher melting temperature, because its genome is about 66% G plus C and G-C pairs have three hydrogen bonds.
choices.rationale: Correct: In double-stranded DNA, A = T, so species Y has 17% T and G plus C is 100 - 34 = 66%, while species X has 100 - 62 = 38%; more G-C pairs means more hydrogen bonds.

title: predict thermal stability of double-stranded DNA from the number of hydrogen bonds. (variant 3)
stem: Two DNA duplexes each have 50% G-C content. Duplex 1 is 20 base pairs long and duplex 2 is 60 base pairs long. Which statement best predicts which melts at the higher temperature?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They melt at the same temperature, because they have the same percentage of G-C pairs.
choices.rationale: Equal percentage does not mean equal total number of hydrogen bonds, and the longer duplex holds three times as many.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Duplex 2 melts higher, because it has 150 hydrogen bonds compared with 50 in duplex 1.
choices.rationale: Correct: Duplex 1 has 10 x 3 + 10 x 2 = 50 hydrogen bonds and duplex 2 has 30 x 3 + 30 x 2 = 150, so duplex 2 needs more energy to separate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Duplex 1 melts higher, because shorter molecules are more stable.
choices.rationale: Shorter duplexes have fewer hydrogen bonds and separate more easily.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Duplex 2 melts lower, because longer molecules have more A-T pairs.
choices.rationale: Both have the same 50% proportion of A-T pairs, and the longer duplex has more bonds overall.

title: infer whether a nucleic acid is DNA or RNA, and whether it is double-stranded, from base composition.
stem: Nucleic acid is extracted from two sources and the base composition is measured. Source 1: adenine 23%, thymine 23%, guanine 27%, cytosine 27%. Source 2: adenine 32%, uracil 24%, guanine 25%, cytosine 19%. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both sources are double-stranded DNA, because both have bases that sum to 100%.
choices.rationale: Source 2 contains uracil, which occurs in RNA, and its base percentages do not follow the pairing rule.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Source 1 is single-stranded RNA, and source 2 is double-stranded DNA.
choices.rationale: Thymine in source 1 indicates DNA, and source 2 has uracil, so this reverses the assignment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Source 1 is likely double-stranded DNA because A equals T and G equals C, and source 2 is RNA that is probably not fully paired because its percentages do not match in pairs.
choices.rationale: Correct: Equal A and T and equal G and C match base pairing in double-stranded DNA, whereas uracil identifies RNA and unequal percentages suggest a single strand.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Source 1 is RNA because it contains thymine, and source 2 is DNA because it contains uracil.
choices.rationale: Thymine is found in DNA and uracil in RNA, so this pairs each base with the wrong nucleic acid.

title: infer whether a nucleic acid is DNA or RNA, and whether it is double-stranded, from base composition. (variant 1)
stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA from a fish is found to contain 18% thymine. What percentage of the bases is cytosine?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: A = T = 18%, so A + T = 36%; the remaining 64% is G + C, with G = C, so cytosine is 32%.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: 18% is the percentage of thymine and adenine, and cytosine pairs with guanine rather than thymine.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: 64% is the total of G plus C, and cytosine is only half of this.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: 82% is 100 minus thymine and does not account for the pairing of A with T.

title: infer whether a nucleic acid is DNA or RNA, and whether it is double-stranded, from base composition. (variant 2)
stem: A nucleic acid from a virus particle has the base composition adenine 20%, thymine 30%, guanine 25%, and cytosine 25%. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is single-stranded DNA, because it contains thymine but the percentage of A does not equal T.
choices.rationale: Correct: Thymine means DNA, and A is not equal to T, so the molecule is not fully base paired and is probably single-stranded.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is double-stranded DNA, because it contains thymine.
choices.rationale: Double-stranded DNA would have equal A and T, but here they differ, so the molecule is probably not fully paired.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is RNA, because the percentages of adenine and thymine are different.
choices.rationale: RNA contains uracil instead of thymine, and this sample contains thymine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is double-stranded RNA, because G equals C.
choices.rationale: RNA would contain uracil rather than thymine, so the presence of thymine rules out RNA.

title: infer whether a nucleic acid is DNA or RNA, and whether it is double-stranded, from base composition. (variant 3)
stem: A nucleic acid sample has adenine 25%, uracil 25%, guanine 25%, and cytosine 25%. A student concludes it must be a double-stranded RNA. Which response is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The sample is RNA because it contains uracil, but equal percentages alone do not prove it is double-stranded.
choices.rationale: Correct: Uracil identifies RNA, but a single strand can have these percentages by chance, so double-strandedness cannot be proven from composition alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The student is correct, because equal percentages prove pairing between strands.
choices.rationale: A single strand could contain equal amounts of the four bases, so equal percentages are consistent with pairing but do not prove it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The sample must be DNA, because the percentages are equal.
choices.rationale: DNA contains thymine, not uracil, so uracil rules out DNA.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sample must be single-stranded, because RNA is never double-stranded.
choices.rationale: Some RNA viruses have double-stranded genomes, so RNA is not always single-stranded.

title: link denaturation treatments to the levels of protein structure that are altered.
stem: An enzyme is heated to 95°C for 5 minutes and cooled to 25°C. Before heating, the enzyme is active, the amino acid sequence is determined, and a measurement finds that 40% of the chain is in alpha helices. After heating and cooling, activity is zero, the amino acid sequence is unchanged, the molecular mass is unchanged, and helices account for 5% of the chain. Which statement best explains the results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heating broke peptide bonds, which changed the amino acid sequence.
choices.rationale: The sequence is the same after heating, so peptide bonds were not broken.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heating disrupted hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions that maintain secondary and tertiary structure, but left the covalent peptide bonds and primary structure intact.
choices.rationale: Correct: Unchanged sequence and mass show that peptide bonds were not broken, while loss of helices and activity shows the folded structure was disrupted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heating changed the gene that codes for the enzyme, so a new protein was made.
choices.rationale: Heating a purified protein does not change genes or make a new protein, and no DNA is present in the sample.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heating removed amino acids from the chain, which lowered the helix content.
choices.rationale: The unchanged molecular mass shows that no amino acids were removed.

title: link denaturation treatments to the levels of protein structure that are altered. (variant 1)
stem: A purified enzyme is dissolved in a high concentration of urea, which disrupts hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions but not peptide bonds, and the enzyme loses all activity. The urea is then slowly removed by dialysis, and 90% of the activity returns. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The primary structure contains the information needed for the chain to refold into its functional shape once the denaturing agent is removed.
choices.rationale: Correct: Peptide bonds and sequence were never altered, so the chain refolded using the information in its amino acid sequence once the conditions allowed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Urea broke peptide bonds, which formed again when the urea was removed.
choices.rationale: Urea does not break covalent peptide bonds, so nothing needs to reform.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The enzyme had been permanently damaged, because activity can never return after denaturation.
choices.rationale: In this experiment activity returned to 90%, so denaturation was reversible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Urea changed the amino acid sequence, and dialysis restored the original sequence.
choices.rationale: Urea does not change the order of amino acids, so no restoration of sequence was needed.

title: link denaturation treatments to the levels of protein structure that are altered. (variant 2)
stem: A student boils an egg. The clear liquid egg white, which is mostly the protein albumin dissolved in water, becomes an opaque white solid. The student claims the heat must have changed the protein's amino acid sequence. Which response is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The student is correct, because heat rearranges amino acids in the polypeptide.
choices.rationale: Heat does not rearrange the order of amino acids, which are joined by strong covalent peptide bonds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The student is correct, because heat converts the protein into fat.
choices.rationale: Heat does not convert protein into fat, since the chemical composition of a protein stays amino acid based.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The student is incorrect, because heat unfolds the protein and exposes hydrophobic regions, which lets the chains stick together and form a solid, while the sequence stays the same.
choices.rationale: Correct: Cooking denatures albumin by disrupting weak interactions; exposed hydrophobic regions cause aggregation, and the primary structure stays unchanged.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The student is incorrect, because heat has no effect on proteins at cooking temperatures.
choices.rationale: The egg white changes visibly at cooking temperatures, which shows that proteins are affected.

title: link denaturation treatments to the levels of protein structure that are altered. (variant 3)
stem: A stomach enzyme works best at pH 2 but is inactive at pH 8. A related intestinal enzyme works best at pH 8 and is inactive at pH 2. Sequencing shows each enzyme has the same amino acid sequence at pH 2 and at pH 8. Which statement best explains why changing the pH can inactivate an enzyme without changing its sequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Changing pH changes the charges on acidic and basic R groups, which alters ionic and hydrogen-bond interactions and therefore the folded shape.
choices.rationale: Correct: Protonation or deprotonation of R groups changes their charge, disrupting the interactions that hold the tertiary structure, while the sequence remains the same.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Changing pH breaks peptide bonds and shortens the polypeptide.
choices.rationale: The sequence is unchanged at both pH values, so peptide bonds are intact.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Changing pH alters the genes that code for the enzyme.
choices.rationale: Genes are not present in the purified enzyme and pH does not change the protein's sequence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Changing pH removes the carbon backbone from the protein.
choices.rationale: The polypeptide backbone remains intact, and the pH changes only the charges on R groups.

title: deduce the number and linkage of polypeptide subunits (quaternary structure) from gel data.
stem: A protein has a mass of 120 kDa in its native form. On a gel containing a detergent that separates subunits held by noncovalent interactions and unfolds each chain but does not break covalent bonds, the protein gives a single band at 60 kDa. When a reducing agent that breaks disulfide bonds is also added, the protein gives a single band at 30 kDa. Which structure is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One polypeptide of 120 kDa, because the detergent cut it into pieces.
choices.rationale: The detergent used does not cut peptide bonds, so a single 120 kDa chain would give a 120 kDa band.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Four identical 30 kDa polypeptides linked by disulfide bonds into a single unit.
choices.rationale: If all four were linked by disulfide bonds, the band without reducing agent would be 120 kDa.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Four 30 kDa polypeptides, in which pairs are joined by disulfide bonds and the two pairs are held together by noncovalent interactions.
choices.rationale: Correct: The 60 kDa bands show two pairs linked by covalent disulfide bonds, and the 30 kDa band after reduction shows each pair is two 30 kDa chains, giving four chains.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two different polypeptides of 60 kDa and 30 kDa that are held together by noncovalent interactions.
choices.rationale: Only one band size appears under each condition, so the sample does not contain a second type of polypeptide.

title: deduce the number and linkage of polypeptide subunits (quaternary structure) from gel data. (variant 1)
stem: A protein has a native mass of 64 kDa. A gel with detergent but no reducing agent shows two bands of 16 kDa, containing different polypeptides in a 1:1 ratio (equal amounts of each). Adding a reducing agent does not change the pattern. Which structure is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single polypeptide of 64 kDa cut by the detergent into four pieces.
choices.rationale: The detergent does not cleave covalent peptide bonds, so a single 64 kDa polypeptide would stay intact.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two 32 kDa polypeptides joined by disulfide bonds.
choices.rationale: The gel shows 16 kDa bands, not 32 kDa, and the reducing agent changed nothing, so disulfide links are not present.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Four identical 16 kDa polypeptides joined by disulfide bonds.
choices.rationale: The gel shows two different polypeptides, so the four chains are not all identical.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Four polypeptides, two of each of two types, held together by noncovalent interactions with no interchain disulfide bonds.
choices.rationale: Correct: Four 16 kDa chains add to 64 kDa, the pattern is unchanged by the reducing agent so there are no interchain disulfides, and the two bands show two kinds of chain.

title: deduce the number and linkage of polypeptide subunits (quaternary structure) from gel data. (variant 2)
stem: A protein has a native mass of 90 kDa. A gel with detergent shows a single band at 90 kDa whether or not a reducing agent is added. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Three 30 kDa chains linked by disulfide bonds.
choices.rationale: Disulfide-linked chains would run at a smaller size after the reducing agent was added, and no change was seen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Three 30 kDa chains held by noncovalent interactions.
choices.rationale: Noncovalent subunits would separate in the detergent and give a smaller band.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two polypeptides of 45 kDa held together by noncovalent interactions.
choices.rationale: Two 45 kDa chains held noncovalently would give a 45 kDa band in the detergent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A single polypeptide of 90 kDa, with no quaternary structure.
choices.rationale: Correct: The protein stays at its native mass under conditions that separate noncovalently or disulfide-linked chains, so it is one polypeptide.

title: deduce the number and linkage of polypeptide subunits (quaternary structure) from gel data. (variant 3)
stem: An antibody has a native mass of 150 kDa. On a gel with detergent but no reducing agent it gives one band at 150 kDa. With a reducing agent, it gives two bands at 50 kDa and 25 kDa, and the 50 kDa band is twice as intense by mass as the 25 kDa band. Which structure is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Four identical 37.5 kDa polypeptides joined by noncovalent interactions.
choices.rationale: The bands observed are 50 and 25 kDa, not 37.5 kDa, and the 150 kDa band without reducer shows covalent linkage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two 50 kDa chains and two 25 kDa chains linked by disulfide bonds.
choices.rationale: Correct: Without reducer the whole molecule stays together, so chains are covalently linked; the reducing agent releases 50 and 25 kDa chains, and 2 x 50 + 2 x 25 = 150 kDa.

choices.label: C
choices.text: One 150 kDa polypeptide that breaks when the reducing agent is added.
choices.rationale: A single polypeptide is not broken by a reducing agent, which cleaves disulfide bonds rather than peptide bonds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Three polypeptides of 50 kDa each held together by noncovalent interactions.
choices.rationale: Three 50 kDa chains would add to 150 kDa, but this ignores the 25 kDa band and a noncovalent assembly would separate in detergent.
